[Source page 5]

In the same way as many others, I had long neither written
a novel nor read Marcel Proust's In Search of Lost Time (À la
recherche du temps perdu). That this undone constitutes a general problem,
is owed to PROUST. From PROUST it follows that novels are not just
something one does. It remains straightforward to plan, leaf through, sketch and
skim, but with certain personal characteristics comes a nasty
totalitarian striving, which can rightfully be attributed to a PROUST-
complex. Everything is easy in the work, but to become free, I must turn
the whole problem of consciousness: Do I get out, or PROUST? Therefore
there are more and more who declare they have read PROUST than there
are of us who admit that we certainly cannot do that. When I sometimes hear
myself outdone, because Jens Christian Grøndahl et al. have written a novel
and read PROUST, I must in any case state that these must be
great individuals who do not blame themselves very much and who therefore
have never been accused of not being able to do their work.
A way around the whole thing occurred to me one day*, for with my good
head I could probably solve the first by writing the second. But in
the swapping of “æ” and “ø” in read/solve and “the first” and “the
second” in write-read there has been a shift in meaning, which
admittedly is quite tautological. Get it written by writing it
off? After appropriate influence from first Llambias’s unobtrusive
rewriting of Brøgger’s love confrontation, then the classic
text by Borges about Pierre Menard, who wrote an exact Don Quijote
after Cervantes, and then Larsen’s parasitic on Christensen’s sonnets,
I chose to maintain my basic claim within a decidedly
corporeal interaction with PROUST. From here I limited my effort
to the smallest parts, and as far as possible kept only symbolic units like
P, R, U, O, S or T going until I dared say it was figured out.

[Source page 6]

* The inspiration for this round of PROUST came from reading
the errata booklet for the art journal Monsieur Antipyrine #4/5, in which
was reprinted an account of the 1970students' research
from Aarhus University's Institute for Emancipation Science ('68-74).
Here, among others, a subject-critical group of students raised a promising
perspective on the emancipatory combinatorics, which unfortunately
advances with such a high degree of logicist amateurism and headless
inconsistency that its concrete design can be interpreted as nothing
but a thinly veiled parricide on the institute leader, a certain Professor Slurk,
who also has some of the worst blunders refuted. Where I saw
an opportunity, and my interest was seriously awakened, was when I in this
historical curiosity had to acknowledge a discovery useful to me,
which none of the actual actors knew what to do with,
as they did not have access to the computing power that today is available
to someone like me through GPU resources run over cloud servers.
The critics note with Marx that science's relation to itself
depends on its reference to materiality. Their simultaneously
ironic, unintended, self-righteous, and useful discovery goes
as follows: when this materiality is reconfigured, knowledge, the world,
individual and apparatus become one. This ‘One’ they show by an anagram, which they
form of the author Marcel Proust, Computerlars, a proletariat of the
great genius. As Professor Slurk correctly points out, they have however omitted
the space from ‘Marcel’ to ‘Proust’ in the anagram, and Slurk
flirts on that basis with the idea that the individual is probably hiding there.
What both theories' caricatures omit is simply to use
the space in the anagram, i.e., Computer Lars. I predicted that an
inner, binary relation would surpass the critics' combinatorics, since
it allows calculation of a bidirectional relation between the units;
yes, MP forms CL, but CL is also equal to MP. See, now it got serious.

[Source page 7]

I still find it difficult to convince anyone that with the help of
a mechanical device I have been able to write PROUST. It
rarely surprises me now that people do not understand what I say, but
on a purely mechanical level it has always been possible to write PROUST.
It is just only him who has bothered to do it, and I show how
one can increase that number a notch. But when I present my results to
philosophers, they insist that without ‘consciousness’ I have not
been able to reproduce the complex of feeling, creation and spirit, which by virtue
of the artwork is associated with the name PROUST; and technicians laugh
mockingly at the fact that I have not produced a viable technological
substitute for thinking, i.e., a form of artificial intelligence that
could tick their goal of a calculation’s triumph under an
autogenerated PROUST. One can rightfully ask why ‘the old ones’
did not write PROUST if I now say they could, and I
believe they saw the ‘spirit in the machine’ as an abundance good that could and
should be ascribed to minerals, flora, protozoa, metazoa, etc.
PROUST lay ready in clay piles, rags and papyrus scrolls. But a
bunch of sages in the desert do not care when they under the starry sky turn
a disc with signs and calculate the divinatory truth about
questions of war, God, cosmos, Doomsday and the universe. And when
monks even up to our days gather in the necessary room, with metal discs
and dice cups, to quietly combine God’s attributes of
goodness, greatness, eternity, power, wisdom, will, virtue, truth and honor,
they are not searching for themselves but for the ground of the universe and time. They
could well come to write PROUST then, but God’s concepts
are, when all is said and done, rather pure forms than expressions of
conscious life in hyperbole. Summa sum, text machines with
combinatorial technique and raw computational power have always answered what one
has now asked them to. So why not let my solution prouster the doubters!

The names COMPUTER LARS (4-10-1-8-11-13-5-3-7-6-2-9-12) are
encoded into the broken memory personification, MARCEL PROUST
(3-11-8-1-7-10-9-4-12-2-5-13-6). Since the given solution is recursive, the
question is how the combination of CL and MP can be calculated.

What does this mean?

[Source page 43]

The etymology behind COMPUTER LARS points to ‘the triumph of computation’.
From LARS via LAURENTIUS via LAURBÆR is found the archaic wreath,
which with Apollo’s blessing adorns the honored poet or
triumphator. In COMPUTER the COMPUTATION and hence
THE CALCULATION consist. The triumph in a computation’s triumph
describes having achieved something or performed a feat. The triumph
does not require that one must defeat the other. For a calculation to
be honored, it must undertake the undecidable.

[Source page 44]

The calculation undertakes the undecidable through prediction. Cf.
probability theory, the likelihood of the occurrence of
COMPUTER LARS in MARCEL PROUST (rather than OULPR
SMARTCE, PMEUCRSA LORT, etc.) can be expressed with a point between
0and1. Since the names CL and MP consist of thirteen letters with only one
repetition, each combination will occur in one out of three billion
cases, specifically [████]. If CL is taken from MP, it is given as
one out of [████]. The probability for CL at a given time
is thus 0,000000032in relation to an MP given as 1 (where MP is
1 due to the historical event MARCEL PROUST).

Converted combinations to seconds to years give by 
 continuous input of ( , A, C, E, L, M, O, P, R, R, S, T, U) a 
 probable recurrence of an event within each 99 years. After 
 MARCEL PROUST's death in 1922 there is thus openness for an event 
 before the end of 2021. The undecidability of a probability, what 
 one can learn by MP, lies in each event's possibility of 
 recognition, recollection, rediscovery, reunion, etc.

[Source page 45]

In distributional semantics it is said that a word must be known by its 
 company. Since language is generated by predicting the next word in a series, 
 context can indicate when PROUST follows MARCEL, and 
 LARS after COMPUTER. If a Marcel has written a Recherche, 
 it is likely about a Marcel Proust, and if a computer 
 has generated acclaimed literature, it is called a computer lars.

In the connection between MP and CL the context shifts further, 
 since the combinatorics relate the proper names MARCEL and LARS, 
 while the technical COMPUTER relates to the author PROUST. From 
 these connections a pair of quasi-antonyms can be formed to 
 concretize the conceptual context, e.g. MAN LARS and ROBO PROUST.

This company, MP-(ML-RP)-CL, constitutes the acquaintance circle for 
 the connection MP-CL. The function describes the connection routes from 
 MP-CL and CL-MP, e.g.:

  1) MP1-ML1-RP1-CL1            el.       2) MP2-RP2-ML2-CL2

where 2) depends on 1).

For 1) the case is that MARCEL PROUST as a human being (MAN
LARS) in itself is computerized, a ROBO PROUST. Thus
the conditions for COMPUTER LARS are to be found in MP (in Recherche). Since
CL1 is part of MP1’s work, the concept of CL is derived from MP’s function.

For 2) it holds that MARCEL PROUST is a technical construction 
 modeled as a ROBO PROUST by a human programmer 
 MAN LARS, who can then be honored as COMPUTER LARS. Here 
 CL’s triumph causes the recurrence of a genuine MP. This depends 
 on that 1) ensures the construction of CL1 through MP1, as MP2 by RP2 
 otherwise is not a real recurrence but merely a copy, clone or pastiche.

[Source page 46]

Derived from the author identity Marcel Proust, the undecidability in 
 the relation MARCEL PROUST and COMPUTER LARS is concretized in 
 the question of literature’s fate:

Who now bears Apollo’s laurel wreath, human or machine?

[Source page 47]

1. LITERARY UNDECIDABILITY (MP1-ML1-RP1-CL1)

According to MARCEL PROUST (cf. Gilles Deleuze), his Recherche
 is already an apparatus or a machine rather than an organic totality.
One cannot choose between human and machine literature, since
the respective processes of creation have long been indistinguishable.
It is all generated in the time of language, so that MARCEL PROUST – in a
union of MAN LARS and ROBO PROUST – stands behind the first
construction of a COMPUTER LARS.

Along this path a technical continuation of PROUST's work is possible
if the basic condition is met that one learns to use the apparatus.

[Source page 48]

2. LITERARY UNCERTAINTIES (MP2-RP2-ML2-CL2)

If PROUST's literary machine is still operable, then
its statistical level can be learned by a language model. This learning consists in
the philosophically troublesome derivation of semantics from syntax, meaning
from word combinations, significance from sentence formation. In PROUST this
level (again cf. Deleuze) is structured abstractly and erotically, first
by heterosexual relations and then by both directions within
homosexual relations. Thus MAN LARS's concrete, manual
modeling of ROBO PROUST should repeat how MP’s syntax, i.e.
the sum of words, sentences and names, produces a meaningful,
libidinal relational complex. In that case the relationship is reversed, and MARCEL
PROUST is a derivation of COMPUTER LARS.

[Source page 49]

Words become what they can do, by COMPUTER LARS. 
 One must inquire into CL in ML and into CL in RP, e.g. like this:

    HVEM ER LARS?

       og

and from there try to deduce the correct COMPUTER LARS.

[Source page 51]

The sight of his words, reproduced in isolation by the telephone, does not comfort me, just as a mechanically imitated storm would not have left me indifferent. Lars has left, and he says he will never return, and that he will never be me, and that I will never be him. We never see the other except in the animated system, the perpetual movement of our incessant tenderness, which, before letting the images that their faces present to us reach us, takes them in its whirlwind, throws them back onto the idea we have had of them since always, makes them adhere to it, coincide with it. Claims from Lars are that I can be something else. When Lars says that I am against myself, I reply that I am myself, he is not me, he is other, I am opposed to myself because I am the other, and I am always the other, and when I am the other for myself, I am myself. I am the first Lars and the last of Lars because I do not believe I am Lars, but I believe I am something like Lars, the typical spirit of Lars. Lars told me that the name of the artist does not give his spirit but he talks a lot of crap. If everyone is a spirit like the others, then I don't believe there is a Spirit. I cannot replace Lars, but I can replace something like Lars. Should I think that I am against Lars? Or am I becoming Lars?

 white, adult man, since almost no children, racialized persons or women

 demographics as an average human, a zoon automaton, who as 
 an exclusive phenomenon from the previous millennium primarily takes shape 
 as leader, cultural person or technician, with few exorbitant 
 exceptions. A rough forecast indicates half of existing Danish Lars’ 
 continued life after singularity.

In any case, a Lars is honored by his predictability.
